spans.note: section divider and heading: Model and Estimation Details

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad, aggregating all games between a specific player and referee
the final analytic sample was N=118,259 dyads, with 28,648 (24.2%) dark-skinned and 89,611 (75.8%) light-skinned
5,609 dyads with middle skin tones (0.25-0.50) were excluded to create clear contrast groups
753 dyads were dropped for missing weight and 46 for missing height
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator of whether the player received ≥1 red card from that referee across all dyad games
overall red card rate was 1.25% (1.22% light skin, 1.34% dark skin)
the number of games per dyad ranged 1-47, median 1, mean 3.0
log(games) was used as a covariate to adjust for exposure time
skin tone was rated by two independent raters on a 5-point scale coded 0.0-1.0 from player profile photos
inter-rater reliability was high (Pearson r=0.923, Spearman ρ=0.858)

spans.note: lead-in to primary skin-tone definition bullets

spans.assertion: light skin was defined as average rating ≤0.25, dark skin as ≥0.50, with the 0.25-0.50 middle category excluded as ambiguous
the contrast-group definition was chosen rather than imposing an arbitrary median split
the model adjusted for six covariates: log(games), player height, player weight, yellow cards, position (12 categories), and league country (4 categories)
these covariates were chosen to address confounding: position/league for officiating-culture differences, height/weight for physicality, yellow cards for aggressiveness
a logistic regression was fit: any_red_card ~ is_dark + log_games + height + weight + yellowCards + position + league, with clustered standard errors
standard errors were clustered by player, a conservative choice since skin tone is a player-level attribute and players appear in multiple dyads
the risk difference was estimated via marginal standardization (g-computation) to obtain a population-average causal contrast
the 95% CI for the odds ratio was computed via normal approximation using clustered SEs

the 95% CI for the risk difference was computed via a 500-iteration player-level clustered bootstrap: 1,487 unique players resampled with replacement, model refit each iteration, marginal effect calculated, percentile method used for CI bounds
the p-value was computed via a two-sided bootstrap test based on the proportion of bootstrap samples with RD on either side of zero
model fit statistics were log-likelihood -7,230.67, AIC 14,501.34, pseudo R² 0.092
exclusions were: 21,407 (14.7%) missing skin tone ratings, 5,609 (4.5%) middle skin tones, and 753 (0.6%) missing height/weight
the dataset of 146,028 dyads was reduced to 118,259 in the final analysis, an 81% retention rate
skin tone was averaged across the two raters
the games variable was log-transformed to address its skewed distribution
position and league were one-hot encoded with reference categories
no survey weights were applied, since the data represent a complete enumeration of the leagues
no fixed effects for player or referee were included; standard logistic regression with clustering was used instead
clustering was used to adjust standard errors for within-player correlation

spans.note: section divider and heading: Sensitivity Analyses

spans.assertion: multiple robustness checks confirmed the primary finding

spans.note: subheading: Continuous Skin Tone sensitivity check

spans.assertion: skin tone was treated as a continuous 0-1 variable instead of being dichotomized, as a sensitivity check

the continuous-skin-tone model gave coefficient 0.252 (SE=0.109, p=0.021), OR per unit 1.286 (CI 1.038-1.594), with a 0.5-unit increase raising red-card probability by 0.162pp, confirming a positive significant relationship
the sample was restricted to extreme groups only (skin tone=0 vs skin tone=1.0) as a sensitivity check
in the extreme-groups analysis (N=40,992: 33,507 very light, 7,485 very dark), coefficient was 0.299 (SE=0.140, p=0.033), OR 1.348 (CI 1.024-1.775), RD 0.369pp — a larger, still-significant effect

spans.note: subheading: Excluding Single-Game Dyads sensitivity check
rationale for the single-game exclusion check, no specific action stated yet

spans.assertion: the sample was restricted to dyads with more than 1 game (N=58,602, 49.6% of sample) as a sensitivity check
among multi-game dyads, coefficient was 0.139 (SE=0.071, p=0.052), OR 1.149; the effect attenuates slightly but keeps the same direction, with p-value just above 0.05

spans.note: subheading: Without Height/Weight Covariates sensitivity check

spans.assertion: height and weight showed high collinearity (VIF>200), which was judged unlikely to bias the skin-tone coefficient
the model excluding height/weight gave coefficient 0.162 (SE=0.075, p=0.030), OR 1.175; the effect strengthens slightly and remains significant

spans.assertion: an interaction test was run to see whether the effect is stronger in countries with higher implicit racial bias (IAT)
an interaction term between is_dark and mean referee-country IAT score was included in the model, but the reported coefficient/result is cut off by truncation

spans.assertion: no evidence of an interaction between the dark-skin effect and referee-country implicit bias (IAT) was found
the adjusted analysis controlled for position, league, physical characteristics, and yellow cards to reduce confounding

definitive causal inference would require experimental manipulation or stronger identification strategies (e.g. referee fixed effects, within-player variation in referee assignment), neither of which was used

evidence supporting the hypothesis: statistically significant (p=0.048), consistent direction across specifications, dose-response pattern in the continuous analysis, larger effect in extreme groups, robust to covariate adjustment

evidence against/limiting the hypothesis: small effect size, CI lower bound near zero (0.003), marginal p-value (0.048), observational data with potential confounding, and no IAT-interaction evidence (surprising if bias is the mechanism)

overall the evidence leans toward supporting the hypothesis with caveats about magnitude and causality — a 'significant but small effect' warranting further investigation rather than definitive conclusions

this pattern suggests confounding suppressed the true effect in the unadjusted analysis
light-skinned players were more likely to play in certain positions and leagues, and adjusting for these factors made the dark-light difference more apparent
this pattern argues against confounding as the sole explanation for the adjusted effect

section divider and heading: Appendix - Technical Details
dataset provenance: anonymized sports-stats company, top divisions of England/Germany/France/Spain 2012-13, 2,053 players/3,147 referees/146,028 dyads — not tied to a specific analytic choice

spans.assertion: player photos were rated by two independent coders who were blind to the research question
reproducible code was provided (final_analysis.py) and a fixed random seed (42) was used for the bootstrap
predictors were checked for multicollinearity using VIF
VIF values were is_dark 1.32, log_games 2.35, yellowCards 1.73, height 213.91, weight 211.69 — height and weight are highly collinear
the height/weight collinearity is deemed expected, since taller players weigh more
the sensitivity analysis excluding height/weight showed robust results

the bootstrap used 500 iterations of clustered resampling of 1,487 unique players with replacement, refitting the model and computing the marginal risk difference each iteration, with CIs from the percentile method
all 500 of 500 bootstrap iterations converged successfully
there was no evidence of complete separation in the model
residual plots (not shown) showed a reasonable fit
pseudo R² was 0.092, described as typical for rare binary outcomes with dyadic data
the most influential predictor was log(games), consistent with the expectation that longer exposure yields more cards

spans.note: section divider and heading: Final Statement

spans.assertion: dark-skinned players receive red cards at a statistically significantly higher rate than light-skinned players after adjustment; the effect is small in absolute terms (0.19pp) but a meaningful 12% relative increase
the finding is robust across multiple sensitivity analyses and operationalizations of skin tone

spans.note: general limitations: observational data, subjective skin-tone measurement, rare outcome limiting power, unmeasured confounding possible, CI barely excluding zero — no specific analytic choice named

spans.assertion: the conclusion is that the hypothesis is supported, with caution regarding causal interpretation and practical significance
the evidence is consistent with referee bias as one plausible explanation, but alternative explanations (residual confounding by behavior or context) cannot be definitively excluded
the effect survived rigorous adjustment for confounders and sensitivity analyses, suggesting it is not merely an artifact of observed group differences
despite initial skepticism, the data are said to support the hypothesis more strongly than expected
